SS Halder with Bibash Chandra Biswas, Probir Halder, Jahangir Alam and S S Sarker, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.

full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause why the decree passed in Family Appeal No.1 of 1989 by the Family Appellate Court and District Judge, Shariatpur modifying that of the Family Court and Assistant Judge in Title Suit No.1 of 1989 should not be set aside. 

 2. The short fact leading to this Rule is, that the opposite party was married to the petitioner according to Hindu Law. At the time of marriage the father of the opposite party gave Jautuk to the present petitioner and a son and a daughter were born out of their wedlock and subsequently the daughter died. Thereafter in the month of Ashar, 1394 BS the petitioner sent the opposite party No.1 to her father's house and he never maintained her or her child. In the meantime the present petitioner at the instance of the opposite party Nos. 2-4 married for the second time and refused to maintain the opposite party No.1 or her child. With that allegation the opposite party No.1 instituted Family Suit No. 02 of 1989 before the Family Court and Assistant Judge, Naria, Shariatpur and prayed for a decree of maintenance. The suit was decreed with a direction that the present petitioner shall pay Taka 500.00 per month to opposite party No.1 and Taka 300.00 per month to the minor child on account of maintenance for 19 months totalling Taka 15,200.00. 

 3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree, the petitioner preferred Family Appeal No.0l of 1989 before the Family Appellate Court and District Judge, Shariatpur who by his judgment dated 16-8-90 affirmed the decree with certain modifications that the defendant petitioner shall pay to the plaintiff and her son an amount of Taka 300.00 and Taka 200.00 respectively towards their maintenance which will be effective from the date of filing of the suit is 4-2-1989. 

 4.  The petitioner on being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court moved this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 5.  Mr Alimuzzaman Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner pressed this Rule only on the legal point that a Family Court constituted under Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 had/has no jurisdiction to pass such a decree as the parties are Hindus. Mr Chowdhury has not controverted or entered into the merit of the case. It is submitted by Mr Chowdhury that the provisions of Family Courts Ordinance is applicable only to the Muslims. Though in section 1(2) of the said Ordinance it has been mentioned that this law will extend to entire Bangladesh, according to Mr. Chowdhury Section 5 of the Ordinance has put a limit to the jurisdiction of the Courts to entertain a case under this law which has provided that subject to the provisions of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, a Family Court will have exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of any suit relating to or arising out of subjects mentioned in the section. Mr Chowdhury strenuously argued that the words "subject to the provisions of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961" used in section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance clearly indicate that the essential pre-condition for filing a suit in a Family Court is that the parties should only be Muslims. In support of his submissions Mr Chowdhury placed reliance in the case of Balakrishna Chetty and sons vs. State of Madras, reported in AIR 1961 (SC) 1152. Mr Chowdhury further submits that section 5 of this Ordinance should also be read along with section 23 of the Ordinance which will make it clear that this Ordinance is meant only for the persons who profess Islam. He also submits that the Family Court Ordinance has been introduced for the enforcement of the rights of the Muslims only. It is also submitted that the Personal Laws of the Hindus have not been interfered with by any legislation previously and when in section 5 there is mention of dissolution of marriage, dower which are not available to Hindus, it indicates that Family Courts Ordinance is meant only for the Muslims as those rights are only available to them. 

 6. Mr SS Halder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No.1, that is, the decree holder, strangely enough took the line of argument advanced by Mr Alimuzzman Chowdhury giving a go-bye to the case of opposite party No. 1 who succeeded in both the Courts below. Mr Halder without surrendering his power has argued the case against the interest of his client. He never spoke a word on the merit of the suit and the application. Adopting the submission of Mr Alimuzzaman Chowdhury he submits that Family Courts Ordinance is available only to the Muslims. Mr SS Halder submits that Article 41 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh has given a right which is fundamental in nature to the citizen to profess, practice or propagate any religion and the same right cannot be curtailed by promulgating any Act or Ordinance. He submits that the right of the non-Muslims has been curtailed on the promulgation of the Family Courts Ordinance. 

 7. It appears that the Rule was issued by a Single Bench which on 18-1-1995 referred the matter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for constituting a Special Bench for a final decision by the High Court Division in the matter of applicability of the Family Courts Ordinance to different communities as there are two divergent decisions on the point by the High Court Division. A Division Bench decided that Family Courts Ordinance is applicable only to the Muslims and it is reported in 14 BLD 450. In the said BLD at page 413 a Single Bench decided otherwise. Another Division Bench in 47 DLR 18 decided that Family Courts Ordinance is applicable to all the communities living in this country and, as such, this Special Bench was constituted by the learned Chief Justice by his order dated 6-7-1996 and when this Bench took up the matter it felt the necessity of assistance on the point from some senior Members of the Bar and accordingly, Mr SR Paul, Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Mr M Nurullah and Mr BK Das were requested to address the Court as Amici Curiae on the point involved in the matter. But due to illness Mr BK Das failed to address the Court. We have heard at length the three Amici Curiae on the point involved in the matter. 

 8. Mr SR Paul the learned Senior Advocate submitted that the Family Courts Ordinance was promulgated to solve certain internal problems of the Muslims. During his argument Mr Paul traced the background of the promulgation of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance. It is submitted that the personal Laws of the Muslims have been interfered with from time to time since the British period when difficulties arose. He noted that Waqf Validation Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act, etc, were enacted when certain problems cropped up amongst the Muslims and in the same manner, Muslim Family Laws Ordinance was promulgated which brought some changes in the Muslim Personal Laws. It is submitted that previous to Dissolution of Muslim Marriage Act the Muslim wives had no right to dissolve the marriage but this enactment has given some rights to them to that effect and in the same line in the matter of dissolution of marriage, inheritance, etc, Muslim Family Laws Ordinance was promulgated and when after the promulgation of the ordinance it was found that some of the provisions of the Ordinance have been frustrated the Family Courts Ordinance was enacted for giving substantive relief to the aggrieved Muslim party and also for giving effect to the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance. He submits that sections 5 and 23 of the Family Courts Ordinance clearly indicate that the same is meant for the Muslims. Mr Paul also submits that the Family Courts Ordinance was promulgated for expeditious disposal of cases filed by the Muslims. He argued that words “subject to Muslim Family Laws Ordinance” as mentioned in section 5 are indicative of the intention of the legislature. According to him, the five subjects mentioned in section 5 are to be tried in a Family Court and that too where the parties are Muslims. In support of his submission Mr Paul placed reliance in the case of Adnan Afzal vs. Sher Afzal reported in 21 DLR (SC) 123. 

 9. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Senior Advocate appearing as another amicus curiae without supporting the contentions of Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury, SS Haldar and Mr SR Paul submits that if Family Courts Ordinance is intended to apply only to the Muslim community then there was no reason for not providing it accordingly as has been done in case of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961. The Family Courts Ordinance should have been named as Muslim Family Courts Ordinance. He also submits that in the Family Courts Ordinance there was no exclusive exclusion of any community and unless there is specific exclusion the law will have general application that is it will apply to the citizens of all faiths. He submits that there is nothing in section 5 to limit the application only to the Muslim citizens. It is also submitted that exclusive jurisdiction given to the Family Courts in matters specified in section 5 is not limited to the Muslim citizens but subject to provision of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance it applies to all the citizens. He also argued that if sections 3.5 and 24 of the Muslim Family Courts Ordinance are read together it will be evident that guardianship and custody of children were made exclusively triable in the Family Courts and unless the law is applicable to all how a non-Muslim can get a relief in the said matters. Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed also argued that 5 matters enumerated in section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance are matters of personal laws of the citizens of different faiths who follow different rules in matters enumerated in the section or do not have any rule at all as in the case of Dower and Dissolution of Marriage in case of Hindus. All citizens may not be concerned in all matters but that cannot be a ground to hold that the Ordinance applies only to the Muslims. He also argued that Family Courts Ordinance has not encroached upon the personal laws of the citizens of any faith. This  Ordinance provided that Family Courts will have jurisdiction to entertain and decide suits on the matters enumerated in section 5 subject to the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance meaning thereby that while disposing of a matter amongst the Muslim the provision of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance shall have to be kept in mind. It is also argued that the Family Courts Ordinance provided special forum for deciding the matter specified in section 9 irrespective of the faith of the parties and that is meant for expeditious disposal of the cases and it has also provided a procedure for trial of cases in camera if required for maintaining secrecy, confidentiality and for deciding some complicated and sophisticated matters which may not be possible under normal laws of the land. The Code of Civil Procedure except sections 10 and 11 and the Evidence Act have not been made applicable in the proceeding which indicate the anxiety of the lawmakers to dispose of the Family matters in a congenial atmosphere. There is also provision for pretrial meeting of the parties which is also meant for solution of the problems amicably. It is also argued that had there been no exclusive jurisdiction of Family Courts there may be complications in cases filed by husband and wife professing different faiths. Mr Ahmed submitted that the Family Courts Ordinance has only provided a special forum for speedy, healthy and congenial disposal of the Family matters and it is a self contained Code. It is argued that not all the personal laws of the Muslims have been included in section 5. Some provisions of Muslim Personal Laws such as Waqf, Gift, parentage, etc, have been kept out of the provisions of the Family Courts Ordinance. So it cannot be said that this law is only for the Muslims. 

 10. Mr M NurulIah, Senior Advocate and another Amicus Curiae supporting the submissions of Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed added that Family Courts Ordinance does not apply only to Muslims it applies to all communities now living in Bangladesh. He also submits that some subjects of the Muslim personal law such as legitimacy, gift, waqf, will, pre-emption, etc, have not been brought under the purview of Family Courts Ordinance. He submits that section 3 of the Ordinance gives wide powers to decide all matters enumerated in section 5.Mr Nurullah submits that such type of provisions as contained in section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance is not a new concept in the sub-continent. These may be found in West Pakistan Family Courts Ordinance, 1964. He submits that the provision of section 5 of our Family Courts Ordinance is exactly the same as in West Pakistan Family Courts Ordinance 1964 and we may interpret the provisions of section 5 of our Ordinance in the light of the interpretation given by the higher Courts of Pakistan and it is expected that there may be a harmonious interpretation of the provisions of two Ordinances. Mr Nurullah submits that the Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Muhammad Azam vs. Muhammad Iqbal and others reported in PLD 1984 (SC) 95 has held that West Pakistan Family Courts Ordinance is applicable also to non Muslims. That case was in between two Kadianis who were previously officially declared non-Muslims in Pakistan. He also relied on a decision reported in PLD 1971, Karachi, 537 Daphne Joseph vs. Malik Eric Roshan Khan. Mr Nurullah also submits that it may be argued that if the Family Courts Ordinance is not applicable to all citizens irrespective of their faith then why three Hill Districts which are also inhabited by the Muslims have been excluded from the purview of the Ordinance under section 1 (2) providing that Hill Districts of Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachhari will remain out of the ambit of the Family Courts Ordinance. He submits that initially the Hill Districts used to be governed by Hill Districts Regulation of 1900 and though it was repealed in 1983 but as no new law has been introduced for administering the area covered by these districts under the provisions of General Clauses Act the repealed law is still in force and as the Hill Districts. .Regulation is still continuing and the laws meant for the plains have no manner of application the said areas have been excluded from the purview of the Family Courts Ordinance. 

 11. Before we decide the points raised let us look into the law itself. Section 1(2) of Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 provided that it extends to whole of Bangladesh except the three Hill Districts and section 3 provided that the provisions of the Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. The main subject of controversy before us is section 5 which runs as follows: 

 "5 Jurisdiction of Family Courts-Subject to the provisions of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 (VIII of 1961), a Family Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of any suit relating to, or arising out of, all or any of the following matters, namely: a) dissolution of marriage 

 12. Mr Alimuzzamen Chowdhury, Mr SS Halder and Mr SR Paul, the learned Advocates contended that the words "subject to the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance" mean and indicate that this Family Courts Ordinance is meant only for the Muslims. They contended that section 23 also lends support to their views. 

 13. Now we are to interpret what is the meaning of the words "subject to the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance" and whether it extends to Muslims only or includes all the communities living in Bangladesh. Mr Alimuzzamen Chowdhury contends that these words mean the initial pre-condition for invoking the jurisdiction of the Family Courts which has been controverted by Mr Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed and Mr M Nurullah. Mr Alimuzzaman Chowdhury while pressing this point placed reliance in the, case of KRCS Balakrishna Chetty and Sons & Co. vs. State of Madras, reported in AIR 1961 (SC) 1152 and in that case a controversy arose on the interpretation of the words "subject to the provisions" as mentioned in section 5 of Madras General Sales Act where section 3 is the charging section and section 5 gives exemption from taxation but that section clearly makes the holding of a licence subject to restriction and conditions prescribed under the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. It has been held that on a proper interpretation of section 5 the expressions "subject to" only means that the exemption under the licence is conditional upon the observance of the conditions prescribed and upon the restrictions which are imposed by and under the Act whether in the rules or in the licence itself that is, a licensee is exempt from assessment as long as he conforms to the conditions, of the licence and not that he is entitled to exemption whether the conditions upon which the licence is given are fulfilled or not. Mr Alimuzzaman Chowdhury contends that in the case before us when it has been mentioned in section 5 that "subject to the provisions of Muslim Laws Ordinance Family Courts shall have exclusive jurisdiction to try and dispose of suits relating to the five matters enumerated therein, it is only meant for the Muslims. What we have found from the said decision it appears that the Indian Supreme Court interpreted the words "subject to" in the manner that certain conditions that has been enumerated in the instrument or law shall have to be followed. In Family Courts Ordinance by adding the words "subject to" no general precondition has been imposed. This "subject to" is only for the people, professing Islam. While disposing of disputes between Muslim parties the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance shall have lobe followed and that is the only condition imposed under section 5. It is well known that under Muslim Personal Law, a husband has been given the power of Talaq. But under section 7 of Muslim, Family Laws Ordinance some restrictions have been imposed in respect of Talaq. It has been provided that no talaq will be effective unless notice of the same is given, to the Chairman and if the Chairman or the Conciliation Board fail to conciliate the matter, the Talaq will be effective after 90 days though Muslim Personal Law provides that Talaq may be effective then and there. In Family Courts Ordinance a marriage of a Muslim may be dissolved under section 5(a) but for the effective dissolution of the same section 23 provides that if a decree is passed the same should be referred to the local Chairman who will try to conciliate in the matter as per section 7 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance and if he fails within 90 days the decree for dissolution will become effective. Section 23 of the Family Courts Ordinance if read with section 5 will make it clear that the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance shall have to be followed in case of decree passed by the Family Court for the dissolution of a marriage as enumerated, in section 5 (a) of the Ordinance if it relates to Muslims only. The rights and liabilities that have been given to the citizens professing Islam, under Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, it appears, have been fully protected under section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance when the words "subject to the provisions of Muslim Family Laws Ordinance'', has been used. 

 14. It may be noted here that as regards restitution of conjugal rights no such provision has been made in Muslim Family Laws Ordinance and section 23 of the Family Courts Ordinance is also silent on this. Family Court will decide that point in accordance with normal laws of the land and so is the case with dower. It appears from section 5 that the subjects covered by Muslim Family Laws Ordinance shall have to be followed while deciding a case filed for any of the subjects enumerated in Family Courts Ordinance by the Family Courts. Therefore, it is found that only restriction imposed under section 5 is that the subjects mentioned in the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance shall have to be decided by the Family Courts in accordance with that Ordinance as is evident from section 23 of the Family Courts Ordinance. 

 15. While submitting that the provisions of the Family Courts Ordinance is also applicable to the citizens who profess other religions Mr Nurullah cited a decision reported in PLD 1971, Karachi, 537 (Daphne Joseph vs. Malik Eric Roshan Khan) which was decided while disposing of a case filed under West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964. Section 5 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act provides as follows: 

 "5. Jurisdiction of Family Courts-Subject to the provisions' of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 and the Conciliation Courts Ordinance, 1961, the Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of and adjudicate upon matters specified in the schedule. " 

 This provision of section 5 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Ordinance is exactly in the same line with our section 5. There they have also kept the Conciliation Courts Ordinance along with Muslim Family Laws Ordinance. The Karachi High Court in the said decision has held that there is nothing in the Family Courts Act by which it can be made inapplicable to the communities other than Muslims. The words 'subject to' has been interpreted in a manner that while deciding a matter in between two Muslim parties the provisions of two ordinances mentioned in section 5 should be looked into or kept in mind. In our law only one Ordinance has been mentioned which is Muslim Family Laws Ordinance. The Pakistan Supreme Court in the case of Md Azam vs. Md Iqbal, reported in PLD (1989) 95 also entertained an application by the two Kadianies. The gist of this decision is, that the Ordinance is applicable to all citizens irrespective of their faiths. In 21 DLR (SC) 123 (Adnan Afzal vs. Sher Afzal) it has been held that the combined effect of sections 5 and 20 of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act is clearly to give exclusive jurisdiction to the Family Courts without, in any way, diminishing and curtailing the rights already possessed by a litigant with regard to the schedule matters. Agreeing with this decision we hold that while deciding the matters enumerated in section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance of our country the court shall have to protect the pre-existing rights of the litigants. It means the citizens who have their personal laws and rights are very much protected in a proceeding initiated at the Family Court. The Family Court cannot go beyond the personal laws or right of the litigant. What the Muslims got by Muslim Family Laws Ordinance in no way can be curtailed under the Family Courts Ordinance. In this decision it has also been held that the Family Courts Act has only changed the forum, altered the method of the trial and empowered the court to grant better remedies. It has brought only a procedural change without affecting the substantive right. Mr SR Paul relying on this decision submitted that a separate forum has been created and we fully accept his contention. The Family Courts Ordinance has not taken away any personal right of any litigant of any faith. It has just provided the forum for the enforcement of some of the rights as is evident from section 4 of the Ordinance. Here it may be mentioned that the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance has given some rights to the people professing Islam, but no forum has been created under that Ordinance for effective disposal of the matter or mitigating the grievances. The Family Courts Ordinance has created this forum. 

 16. As regards the people professing the religion of Hinduism, it appears that some of their personal laws have been interfered with as far back in 1946 when Hindu Woman's Right to Separate Residence and Maintenance Act, 1946 was promulgated. This law has given a right to the Hindu wives to live in separate houses and to have the maintenance. But no provision was made how to enforce the rights. In any such event the aggrieved party had to take recourse to time consuming Civil Suits. The Family Courts Ordinance has provided a new forum for speedy and effective disposal of the points at issue. According to Hindu Personal Law the wife and the child may get maintenance but no speedy forum was there even 1946 Act has not provided any forum. The Family Courts Ordinance now provided the forum. After the coming into force of Family Courts Ordinance five subjects enumerated therein are made exclusively triable by the Family Court and section 3 of the Ordinance made it available to all citizens irrespective of their faith. If the provisions of sections 6 to 9 and 11 to 16 are considered it would appear that a separate procedure has been provided for the disposal of cases filed in the Family Courts under this Ordinance. So, we are of the view that Family Courts Ordinance is a self-contained Code which gives a forum to the litigants for enforcing their rights in respect of five subjects enumerated in section 5. 

 17. On consideration of the relevant laws, particularly the Family Courts Ordinance, it is clear that this Ordinance has not in any way curtailed or superseded the personal laws of the subjects. The Ordinance only provided a special forum for speedy and effective disposal of the cases which may be filed before the Family Courts as is evident from section 4 thereof which provides that there shall be as many Family Courts as there are Courts of Assistant Judge and the latter Courts shall be the Family Courts for the purpose of this Ordinance. 

 18. Further for appointment of guardians, the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890 is still in force which is applicable to all the citizens of the country and the District Judge was competent to deal with the matter acting as a District Court but now after coming into force of Family Court Ordinance the forum is the District Court has been changed. Section 24 of the Ordinance provided that a Family Court shall be deemed to be a District Court for the purposes of Guardians and Wards Act and it has further provided that in dealing with the matter specified in that Act the Family Court shall follow the Special Provision of that Act and the District Judge has now been made the appellate Court who shall follow the provision of section 17. The petitioner has not disputed this provision of section 24. They have not submitted that this Guardians and Wards Act has intruded into the personal laws of the citizens professing religion other than Islam. This indicates that when any person intended to get an order passed under Guardians and Wards Act he should approach the Family Court as that Court has been given the exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the cases filed under that Act and this has been made a District Court under that Act. If section 24 is read along with section 5 it will be very clear that not only the Muslims but other citizens professing any other religion would avail the forum of the Family Court for settling any dispute arising out of Guardianship and custody of Children as that has the exclusive jurisdiction for this purpose. Keeping sections 3, 5 and 24 as it is no one can approach any other Court for decision on any matter of Guardianship and Custody of Children. This shows clearly that Family Courts Ordinance is not meant only for the Muslims. So, on consideration of this aspect of the matter, we hold that Family Courts Ordinance applies to all citizens irrespective of religion. So giving a harmonious interpretation of the words "subject to" as given by the higher Courts of the sub-continent, we hold that this has not created any embargo in the jurisdiction of the Family Courts in respect of case and suits filed by citizens professing religion other than Islam. But while deciding the cases of the subjects enumerated in section 5 it is clear that Family Courts will follow the personal laws of those subjects. 

 19. Mr. M Nurullah lastly placing the decision reported in 47 DLR 18 (Meher Negar vs. Mojibur Rahman) urged for deciding the question of maintainability of a criminal proceeding that may be filed under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure after the coming into force of Family Courts Ordinance. In this decision a Division Bench has held that the Criminal Courts as usual way entertain a case filed under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance. In the said decision it has been held that in section 5 of the Family Courts Ordinance it has been mentioned that the court shall decide the suits filed in respect of the five subjects enumerated in the section. It has been held that there is difference in between a suit and a case. The difference was found from the Pakistani Act, where in West Pakistan Family Courts Ordinance in section 5 the word "matter" was used and not suit and from this the Division Bench held that Family Courts Ordinance has not created any impediment in the proceeding of the case filed under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The gist of the decision is that one may choose any of the two forums. Mr M Nurullah, the learned Amicus Curiae sought a decision on this point as this involved a substantial question of law concerning all the communities. Mr M Nurullah submits that already in the case of Abdul Khaleque (Md) vs. Selina Begum and State, reported in 42 DLR 450 it has been held that the Family Courts . Ordinance ousted the jurisdiction of the Magistrate to entertain an application for maintenance which is a Family Court matter. 

 20. To decide this point raised by Mr M Nurullah let us consider the provisions of the present Ordinance. Section 3 of the Family Courts Ordinance provides that the provisions of this Ordinance shall have effect notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force and section 4 has provided that all courts of Assistant Judges shall be the Family Courts for the purpose of this Ordinance and section 5 provides that the Family Courts shall have exclusive jurisdiction to entertain, try and dispose of any suit relating to the subjects enumerated in this section which includes maintenance. Those sections clearly indicate the ouster of the jurisdiction of other Courts in dealing with the matters enumerated in section 5 of the Ordinance. Now it may be argued that the word 'suit' as mentioned in section 5 indicates a civil proceeding and the cases filed under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a criminal proceeding. So, there is no ouster of the jurisdiction of Criminal Courts in the matters relating to maintenance. But it is well settled that a proceeding under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is quasi criminal, and quasi civil in nature and this section has given certain powers to the Magistrates to grant maintenance to wives and children who are unable to maintain themselves. Sub-section (1) of section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is quasi civil in nature as order for maintenance is passed under this part. But sub-section (3) is quasi criminal. So, in a word, section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is both quasi civil and quasi criminal in nature. On consideration of the provisions of sections 3, 4, 5, and 27 of the Ordinance we hold that the jurisdiction of the Magistrate is clearly ousted. Before coming into force of this Ordinance maintenance matters used to be decided by the Magistrates acting under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Now section 27 provides that all suits, appeals and other legal proceedings relating to or arising out of any matter specified in section 5 pending in any Court immediately before the commencement of this Ordinance shall continue in the same court and shall be heard and disposed of by that Court as if this Ordinance has not been made. This clearly shows that after the coming into force of the Family Courts Ordinance the Criminal Court's jurisdiction has been ousted in respect of awarding maintenance except in case of pending proceedings. By this provision the Courts were allowed to dispose of pending cases and this further shows that as soon as the Ordinance came into force all matters relating to subjects enumerated in section 5 shall have to be brought before the Family Courts. The similar view was also taken in Pakistani jurisdiction in the case reported in PLD 1969 (SC) 187 (Adnan Afzal vs. Capt Sher Afzal). Therefore, on consideration of the laws and the decisions we hold that ordinary criminal courts have lost jurisdiction to entertain and decide cases that may be filed under section 488 of the Code of Criminal Procedure relating to maintenance after coming into force of Family Courts Ordinance. 

 21. This Rule was issued calling into question the decisions given by the Family Court as well as by the appellate Court in awarding maintenance to opposite party No. 1. Though from the side of the petitioner and opposite party No. 1 nothing has been argued on the merit of the case, but we have looked into the judgment of both the Courts below. It appears that after examination of some witnesses and appreciating the evidence the trial Court passed the decree allowing maintenance to opposite party No.1 and her son. The Appellate Court also, it appears, thoroughly considered the evidence on record and came to the concurrent finding of fact that opposite party No. 1 and her child are entitled to get maintenance. But it has reduced the amount to be paid giving effect from 4-2-89. Excepting this all other findings have been affirmed by the appellate Court. As the decision is concurrent on fact and no illegality could be pointed out by the petitioner we find nothing to interfere in I the matter under section 113(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 Before we conclude we must record our appreciation for the services rendered by the Amicicus Curaies who took great pains in addressing the court on the subject of great public importance.
